Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

A clear-minded person who considers the matter fairly, without bias, stubbornness, or evasion, will see that pure minds and cleansed souls have spoken honestly. They were not stained by the ignorance of earlier ages or by selfishness. They did not leave the path of honoring God, speak falsely, or deceive people. God supported them in knowledge and action with remarkable signs and events beyond ordinary experience, without magic, trickery, or fraud. Yet they firmly taught that this world would come to an end: its roof would split, its heavens collapse, its stars fall and lose their light, its earth be laid waste, its seas burst open, and its mountains move and crumble.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

They insisted on this even though, on the surface, belief in an eternal world would not prevent belief in individual souls surviving their bodies, or in reward and punishment after death. So we must be sure they did not speak from whim, but from true knowledge and sincere belief. At the same time, certain rational proofs show that the maker of the world is one and self-sufficient, free of defect or change. He does not shift from one state to another, grow tired of acting, hold back His giving, or wait for a new will or a suitable time.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

Anyone who creates something to gain a benefit—even for someone else—is incomplete and needs something outside himself. If the benefit made no difference to him, it would not explain why he acted. If it did make a difference, he would gain a perfection he lacked. God is therefore complete in His action and will. His essence contains no added purpose or newly arising will. He has always given, and will always give, mercy and existence without limit. The limitation belongs to us, the children of this world of bodies and matter, a passing home whose inhabitants are unjust to themselves.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

We can reconcile philosophy and religion on this great question only through the insight God gave us: things in the physical world are continually renewed, and their own existence is never free from new events. God’s giving remains; the world changes and passes away at every moment. It lasts as one likeness takes the place of another, like the breaths that sustain a person’s life. We fail to notice this because similar things follow one another so smoothly that we mistake them for one continuous thing.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

A note of warning. A mystic writes in The Essence of Realities that saying “the world is eternal in time” is empty talk. Ask what “the world” means. Does it mean all bodies—the heavens and the elements—or every being apart from God? If it means every possible being, bodies and everything else, including minds and souls, then most things called “the world” do not depend on time for their existence. They must exist before time. How can the world be eternal in time if most of what it includes exists before time?
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

If “the world” means only bodies, it still makes no sense to say bodies have existed for as long as time has existed. That suggests that time existed before bodies. But bodies exist before time, while time follows from them, even if only in rank and dependence. That is the mystic’s argument.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

I say that this argument has a flaw: two things can exist at the same time while one is prior to the other in its own being. Yet after close thought, the mystic’s point proves sound. The relation between time and body is like the relation between matter and form: each depends on the other in a different way. Time helps make a body a particular individual, just as matter’s readiness helps make a form particular. Studying the relation between matter and form shows that both are renewed in existence. A form brings matter into being and completes it, as an active cause brings about its effect. Matter, through its readiness, allows a later form to follow the first. The form needs matter; matter prepares for another form. The form causes matter by acting, while matter causes form by preparing to receive it. So both are renewed in existence.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

The same is true of time and body. Time helps make a body a particular, changing thing, while a body sustains time and allows it to continue. Zaytūn the Elder, whose words we quoted in our discussion of nature, says that matter and form are both renewed: things last because new forms keep appearing, and they pass away because an earlier form gives way to the next. Passing away belongs to both form and matter.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

The mystic continues: “If you say bodies existed from the moment God existed, you make a grave mistake. Many scholars think they have judged more honestly than anyone before them. But you must understand that bodies do not exist where the First Reality exists—not now, not before, and not after. Whoever says the world exists now alongside God is deeply mistaken. Where God is, there is no time or place. He encompasses time, place, and every other being. His existence is prior to the world just as it is prior to these written words; there is no difference between the two.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

“Anyone who distinguishes between these cases is still trapped in doubt and has not freed God from likeness to created things or from time. Such people avoid saying He is in a place, as ordinary people do when they imagine Him as a body among other bodies. But they have not reached the true knowledge that comes to a mystic at the beginning of the path. God is prior to past time just as He is prior to future time. A true mystic knows this with certainty. Scholars cannot grasp it by reasoning alone; otherwise, they would not say that the world’s existence is equal to God’s, any more than they would say that the written letters on this page are equal to God’s existence.”
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

Here is the author’s reply. It is correct to say that the world does not exist with God at the level of God’s own existence. But proof, supported by direct spiritual insight, shows that God exists with the world and with every part of it. The same is true of every complete cause in relation to its effect. Because an effect is limited and depends on its cause, it does not exist at the level of the cause’s own complete being. But the cause is present with its effect at the level where that effect exists, without losing any of its own completeness. Anyone who understands this deeply will gain much. The Qur'an supports this: “He is with you wherever you are”; “He is God in heaven and God on earth”; and “Wherever you turn, there is the face of God.” Other verses and prophetic reports say the same.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

So we return to our point. God, who is beyond time, is present at every time, but is not limited to or tied to any time. God, who is beyond place, is present in every place, but is not confined to it, as those who picture Him like a body claim, nor separate from it, as some scholars claim in trying to show that He transcends place. They have not reached the mystics’ level of knowledge and do not see that their way of separating God from the world can itself limit Him and make Him resemble created things. They imagine that the source of the world’s existence is confined by being stripped of some kinds of existence and set apart from the world.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

Yet the Necessary Being must be necessary in every respect. The One who encompasses all cannot have any state of possibility or need. He is with every existent in every respect, without limitation or multiplicity. He is in everything, yet He is not a thing; He is in every time, yet not in time; He is in every place, yet not in a place. He is all things, yet He is not the things themselves.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power

Praise belongs to God, first and last, and peace be upon our master Muhammad and his pure family. Here ends the second part of divine philosophy and with it the Third Journey of the Four Journeys of the Intellect. We have worked to correct and refine this book as carefully as we could. By God’s grace, it is free of errors except those our eyes missed and our attention failed to catch. May God open the way. — Ibrāhīm al-Amīnī, 1389.

This way of describing speech is clear when the speaker is a possible being. But God, the Necessary Speaker, speaks through His own essence. He is therefore the source of every word that brings things into being, as well as spoken words. His speech is an inner attribute—His own transcendent essence—and it has effects: all complete words and the levels below them come from His essence and express what lies hidden in Him, the deepest of all mysteries. If someone says that God speaks by creating speech, and means by “speech” the intellects, which are His complete words, that is a sound view. The same is true of the view that God has inner speech, if this means that His most holy, simple existence contains all words in one simple reality. This also gives a sound meaning to the saying, “Speech is in the heart; the tongue is a guide to what is in the heart.” — س قده

Calling an attribute a “source” means that it gives rise to the attribute. The argument that speech involves effects because its root means “wound” is a play on words, not a proof. Calling speech an inner, effective quality hints at treating it not as an action that follows God’s essence, but as an essential attribute identical with His essence. This is done by defining speaking as the essence affecting another by making what is within it known. In reality, this reduces to power, an essential quality identical with God. But the same argument applies to every active attribute—creating, bringing things into being, giving life, providing, showing mercy, forgiving, and more. If an action comes from a distinctive feature of its agent, one might describe the agent by that feature: “Creator” and “Provider” could refer to the essence from which creation and provision come. Or one might use those names for the agent as it acts, so the attribute is taken from the action and is additional to the essence. The sound view is that God’s essential positive attributes are life, power, and knowledge; hearing and sight return to knowledge, while the rest are active attributes. We can then explain how the active attributes return to the essential ones by tracing them back to the source from which their actions come. — ط مد ظله

Speech as we use it is a shared sign that grew from social need. People need to tell one another what is in their minds. A person living entirely alone would have no need to speak. Animals also use sounds to communicate according to their social needs, such as mating, feeding or raising their young, and defending themselves. Speech may first have appeared through an action meant to show something. A hen picks up a grain in front of her chicks; they follow and peck at it. She then adds a call to the action. Later, the sound alone is enough for the chicks to understand what she means. Something similar happened with human beings. Sounds came to express different aims, words separated, combinations of words developed, and languages appeared. Through repeated use, spoken signs became so clear that a speaker could convey an idea without first showing the action, and a listener could grasp it without seeing it. This is a brief account of how speech arose among us. Words exist as agreed signs for their meanings, and speaking creates a sign for what is in the speaker’s mind so that someone who knows the language can understand the intended meaning. The sign is conventional because its meaning depends on an agreed convention. But an action truly shows the distinctive nature and perfection of its maker. In this sense, every possible being is God’s speech: it reveals what is within Him. Its existence is like a command addressed to itself, as God says, “When He wills a thing, He says to it, ‘Be!’ and it is.” In relation to other beings, it is like a statement. When a being is complete, it is a complete word of God. God says, “There is no changing the words of God,” and calls Jesus “a word from Him.” — ط مد ظله
Here he means speech as the act of speaking. In the second and third definitions, he means speech in its ordinary sense: what the act produces. — س قده

This hints at Mulla Sadra’s settled view: speech means the complete words, the intellects that exist through God’s creative act. In fact, everything exists through Him. On the Ashʿarite view, which defines a speaker as one in whom speech exists, it is no problem for speech to exist in God, since that view treats all His attributes as additional to His essence. — س قده
“Exists in” is used here because union assumes that there are two distinct things. Their distinction comes from one being related to what receives it. — س قده

That is, existence without letters or sounds. The Commander of the Faithful said that when God wills something to exist, He says “Be!”—not as a sound that strikes the ear or a call that can be heard. God’s speech is His act. The author also uses “word” for the fixed realities of possible beings before they receive actual existence. Their being heard is their established presence, as explained in the discussion of knowledge. — س قده
The first difference is between existence and what a thing is, as the mind distinguishes them. The second is their unity in reality. — س قده

According to the list in Sayyid’s Jadhawāt, the intellect, the soul, the nine spheres, the four elements, the three kinds of offspring, and the world of images make nineteen levels—the same number as the letters in the phrase “In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.” Add the nine kinds of qualities, and the total is twenty-eight. — س قده

The intellects are absorbed in existence, like a letter that cannot stand alone as a meaning. Souls are like names: their existence is connected to their own selves and does not disappear into another. Flowing natural powers and changing bodies are like verbs, or acts. — س قده

One might object that this is the highest kind of human speech, yet the person here is listening and receiving, not speaking. First, he speaks with God by asking through his readiness to receive knowledge and understanding from Him; conversation goes both ways. Second, even though these words are first and directly attributed to God or to an angel, they can also be attributed to the soul, as something is attributed to what displays it. They descend from the soul’s inner self to its outward side, the intellect. — س قده
This refers to the prophets. For others, the Prophet said, “Among my community are those who are spoken to and inspired.” — س قده

Taken broadly, Ibn Arabi’s words include the general intellectual knowledge of the rational soul. But his way of speaking and the context suggest that he means the knowledge of people of the heart and the divine promptings received by those on the spiritual path. They describe four kinds of inward prompting. A divine prompting, sometimes called a “knock on the heart,” never errs; it can be recognized by its strength and the way it cannot be pushed aside. An angelic prompting, or inspiration, urges a person toward something required or recommended. A prompting from the self, or an impulse, serves the person’s own interests. A satanic prompting, or whisper, urges a person away from what is right. God says, “Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to do what is shameful.” These promptings can be hard to distinguish in matters where either choice is allowed. What goes against a person’s own desire is more likely to come from the first two; what agrees with it is more likely to come from the last two. By God’s help, a sincere person with a clear heart and attention turned to the truth can tell the difference. — س قده
Far from it! A report from the noble descendants of the Prophet says: “The Holy Spirit tasted the first fruits from the gardens of Ṣāqūra in our gardens.” — س قده

By “the Book,” he means the lowest level of the books written on heavenly tablets: the world of bodies. He reads “There is nothing fresh or dry that is not in a clear Book” as referring to literal opposites such as fresh and dry. — س قده

This means the tablet of breath—nafas, with a vowel on the f—and breath or air taken without restriction, as belonging to the soul—nafs, with the f unvowelled. In the first case, the book was treated as something separate from the soul. In the second, the forms written on the air or on paper are counted as existing through the rational soul. — س قده

It may seem that the passage first calls the breath or air a writer, then says the rational soul is the maker. The two statements fit together: “soul” here means the breathing soul, the soul as it breathes. At this lower level, the breathing soul makes the images and writes them on what receives them. — س قده

When the light of reality appears, nothing else has independent existence, much less a relation to God of either kind. Any relation that assumes separation is only the relation of reality to appearance, or else no real relation at all. This is why Avicenna says that the First has no relation to things; rather, things are related to Him. If things are the subject of the statement, God is their necessary ground, so they must be related to Him. But if God is the subject, things vanish because their existence is borrowed, and no relation remains. The verse “His are the creation and the command” does not prove an ordinary relation. It may mean that He is the preserved source and foundation of all, or that all things receive existence from Him. The better proof is that the one who gives something cannot lack what He gives. — س قده

This is also reported from the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī. The sages say that times and things in time relate to higher principles as the present moment does, and places and things in place as a point does. Events that follow one another in time all exist together in eternity. They explain this with a rope or piece of wood, colored differently along its length, passing in front of an ant whose narrow field of sight cannot take it all in. The colors appear to the ant one after another, but you see them all at once because your sight can take in the whole length. This applies when we look at the world’s forms and what receives them. But if we look at its meaning and existence, there is no extension or sequence at all. Existence has no parts, so it has no size, quality, measure, or number that could divide it into past, present, and future. There is no absence or presence, years or eternities, beginning or decay, return or recurrence. All of these apply only to the things that receive existence and to the forms in which it appears. The Persian verse says: “The water in this stream has changed many times, yet the moon and stars remain in its reflection.” — س قده

In both the outer world and the human inner world, there are four things: an inward Throne and Footstool, and their outward forms. In the outer world, the inward ones are the universal intellect and universal soul; the outward ones are the outermost sphere and the sphere of the fixed stars. In the human inner world, the inward ones are the inner heart, or detailed intellect, and the inner chest, or imagination. Their outward forms are the pine-cone-shaped heart and the brain. — س قده

The effect that reaches the storehouse of imagination is the image in the faculty itself. The lower effect mentioned here is the image in the subtle bodily spirit, which carries the imaginative faculty and displays it. — س قده

This refers to the circular path of the words. When the ear hears what the tongue says, the words return to their source and circle back on themselves, like the creative words through which things come to be. For this reason, some may prefer speaking remembrance of God aloud to silent remembrance, though silent remembrance is better in some respects. — س قده

“Good words” means the complete words: the simple, higher intellects in the upward order of existence. Good action—the religious law and the path of life—raises them. But the meaning that best supports the author’s point is that all beings are God’s words, considered in their luminous aspect. “Good action” then means their inner and outward movements toward greater completion. In this sense, creation itself worships God, as He says, “Your Lord has commanded that you worship none but Him.” This does not conflict with the fact that some beings turn away from Him in their religious conduct. — س قده

Just as a servant in the ordinary sense owns nothing, and everything in his hands belongs to his master, so the true servant’s being, attributes, and actions belong to the Lord of all masters. This follows from the unity of God’s essence, attributes, and actions. God is called the All-Merciful here because His mercy reaches everyone, while His special mercy is for those who believe in and know His oneness. “He has counted them one by one”: just as a final sum gathers all the separate numbers, God’s knowledge gathers all scattered beings in a simpler, higher way, and nothing lies outside it. “Each will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection”: when beings rise from the things that receive them and stand before the One, each is stripped of what is foreign to its own reality. At a minimum, this means leaving behind the worldly body and its attachments—in short, the limits of nature. Complete freedom from matter belongs only to the closest servants of God. A Persian verse says: “Today, yesterday, the day before, and tomorrow—all four become one in tomorrow.” This return to the All-Merciful takes place only in human form, since the human being is the gateway to God and the straight path to Him. The Qur'an guides people to what is most upright: to reflect God’s greatest name. Since God’s giving never ends, every natural being reaches the natural human being and enters through this gateway; all strongholds reach the greatest stronghold, and all villages reach the mother city. Mulla Sadra adds another way to understand this: beings enter the human being through their many relations to him, in his imagination and in the connected worlds of dominion and intellect. In short, when the perfect human being reaches the highest end, all beings reach it with him. This does not mean that each kind of being fails to reach its own Lord and is not gathered to God along with that Lord. — س قده

This passage concerns detailed knowledge, which gives rise to many things within unity, and mercy as an attribute, which gives rise to mercy in action. His words about the appearance of God’s names and about what He first brought into being point to this. He is not speaking of God’s essential knowledge at the level of absolute oneness, or of His essential speech, which is simple and one. Although that knowledge contains all good things in a single, complete act of knowing, that is not the subject here, as his words make clear. — س قده

“Like them” may refer only to the number of earths matching the seven heavens, or it may mean that the earths are heavens too. This is understood when the soul learns what the realities of the heavens are, whether they exist, and why they exist, through descriptions that match them. Things are present in the mind through their own realities; what distinguishes one thing from another is also connected to what they share. The phrase may instead refer to the soul, heart, intellect, and the remaining levels of the human being, which are counted as seven, as will be explained later. In that reading, the unseen world of God’s command descends between these levels. — س قده

“Two days” may mean the moment that has passed—the moment of passing away—and the moment that is coming—the moment of coming into being. Every changing thing in nature is in this state. The phrase may also mean a bright day, seen from God’s side, and a dark day, seen from the self’s side; the days of form and matter; or a timeless day in the world of images and the day of natural time. “He revealed to each heaven its command” means the spiritual word that belongs to the unseen world of God’s command. — س قده

The Tablet may be the Tablet of Decree, where detailed knowledge is held—the world of the governing principles of different kinds, each letter containing all the letters of creation. It may also be the Tablet that records existence. Each letter of creation, as an item of knowledge, is greater and higher than Mount Qaf as an object known. — س قده

“Whoever knows himself knows his Lord” can be understood in several ways. Whoever knows the Prophet, who has a greater claim on believers than they have on themselves, knows his Lord, because the Prophet said, “Whoever has seen me has seen God.” The Prophet’s spiritual reality is the Universal Intellect, the fullest manifestation of God; in his all-embracing nature, he displays God’s Greatest Name. Or it may mean that whoever knows his own soul, created in the image of the All-Merciful and able to embody all the divine names when fully developed, knows his Lord. Knowing an effect as an effect, or a sign as a sign, is knowing its cause and what it points to—especially when the effect is a mirror of its source and has no independent standing. Or it may mean that whoever recognizes his own helplessness and knows that all power belongs to God knows God’s power and its reach. Whoever sees his own ignorance—once an empty mirror and blank page, later adorned with knowledge from God, the Wise and Knowing—knows God’s knowledge of all things, general and particular: “They do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills.” Whoever knows himself as a servant, poor and owning no existence, quality, or action of his own, knows God as Lord, Master, and Self-Sufficient. A fourth reading is that whoever sees how his small world contains all levels—spiritual and bodily, angelic and satanic, with something in him like an angel, a sphere, a plant, an animal, and a devil—knows how the great world contains every level, from the smallest speck to the tiniest particle. A fifth reading describes something impossible: if a limited, ever-changing person could know the full reality of his own self, whose states and aspects cannot be counted, he would know the full reality of his Lord. But that cannot happen. In short, God has a hidden reality that no creature can grasp, and a manifest side known through Him. The soul too has a hidden reality beyond our grasp and a manifest side through which its powers and levels are known. A Persian verse says: “Knowing your soul is no small matter; know God, and you will know what it is.” — س قده

This difference between the Qur'an and the other books follows the difference between their messengers: God gave some messengers a higher rank than others. Since our Prophet is the last in both the order of existence and the line of prophets, no intermediary remains between him and God. The Qur'an is therefore God’s speech, and Gabriel’s role in bringing it down in portions does not contradict this. Other prophets had one or more intermediaries. The two conditions that make speech direct—its independence from what receives it and its direct dependence on the true speaker—were fully and steadily present in the Prophet, so no possible being could surpass him. God says, “Remain upright as you have been commanded.” — س قده
“God’s own speech” means that “God’s” qualifies “speech.” It does not mean that the Qur'an is speech but not a Book. As we have already seen, every speech is also a Book in one respect. — س قده

The earlier distinction between speech and Book was based on whether they depend on matter. This distinction between Qur'an and Criterion is broader: it concerns what is one and what is many. The many may be different kinds of things or ideas, as with different intellects or divine names and attributes; or it may lie in different levels of existence, which vary in strength. The word “Qur'an” comes from a root meaning “to gather,” as in the verse, “Its gathering and its recitation are upon Us; when We recite it, follow its recitation.” The speech sent down to our Prophet is the Universal Intellect, his station and spiritual reality: the whole order of intellects that move the heavens and earth, from their beginnings to their ends. This speech is Qur'an in that it gathers things together; it is Criterion in that it distinguishes their kinds and levels. — س قده

Whatever appears to the senses is perceived, whether it comes from outside or from within. Some followers of the philosophers go beyond saying that the Prophet’s reality connects with the angel’s reality. They say he also connects with the angel’s subtle form through imagination. They do not reduce this to an empty dream: they say the image comes down from the higher Tablets and reflects what is there, like the images in a true dream. Yet this account still falls short. The inner powers are like mirrors facing one another. When an image appears in imagination, it is also reflected in the common sense, which is like a mirror with two faces: one receives images from the outward senses, and the other receives what comes from the higher Tablets or from the imagination. Once we know that the image passes from the inner worlds to the illuminated imagination, then to the common sense, and from there to the senses, how could it fail to be truly seen? The Prophet’s intellect is above the other intellects, and his senses are more luminous than ordinary senses. — س قده

That is, these relational forms give rise to the angels of the Tablets. I suspect the text originally read, “From them come the written angels after they have been measured,” matching the description of these forms as created and measured. The next words refer to the angels of the Tablets. — س قده

The angel also has a subtle aspect that relates to the lower world. Its reality at the high station appears to the Prophet as a pure form in the world of subtle images. That is what is meant by its ascent and descent; it does not mean that it moves through space. The Qur'an says, “The angels and the Spirit descend,” and, “The command descends between them.” Many similar verses express the same idea. — س قده

When the holy spirit of a saint, or someone below a prophet, speaks with angels while awake, the person’s powers do not follow the spirit as fully as a prophet’s powers do, because the saint’s spirit is not as strong as the Prophet’s. The powers remain caught up in sensory distractions, and the spirit cannot pull them away completely. When the Prophet’s spirit meets the angels in sleep, by contrast, his powers follow it, despite his seeming daze, and see what it sees. He is also awake in the natural world: he sees the angel’s form with his senses and hears its voice, recognizing it as an angel. This is one of the marks of prophecy. — س قده

Written, spoken, mental, and outward existence are all appearances of one reality, whether in its full form or its subtle counterpart. The nature of a thing remains itself, and existence has one root; the differences are in strength and weakness. A shadow is not separate from what casts it, a name is not separate from what it names, and a subtle form reflects the reality it represents. In brief, the Qur'an has three forms: the written copy between its covers, and the created signs in the outer world and within the soul. Whoever reads any one of these properly is, in a sense, reading the other two. — س قده

This applies if Mount Qaf means the mountain said to surround the world—the world of subtle images, which branches into Hurqalya, Jābalqā, and Jābarsā. It does not apply if Qaf means God’s power or the heart, since nothing is greater than the heart, as the sacred report says: “My earth and My heaven do not contain Me, but the heart of My faithful servant contains Me.” The mountain may also point to the sacred existence of the final Prophet, Muḥammad. Ibn ʿAbbās said that Qaf is a mountain in Mecca. In this reading, it points to the Prophet’s great standing with God, his firmness on God’s path, and his place between the oneness of God and the many things in creation. — س قده
This applies to every form of the Qur'an, written and created, in the outer world and within the soul. Each can be called by one of its noble names, depending on how it is viewed. — س قده
This means that actual beings are also gathered in the written dot, if the written dot is understood as a subtle counterpart and appearance of the real point in the world of writing. — س قده

This refers to the saying, “Read and rise.” A person moves from the outward meaning to the inward one, and from the inward meaning to its source. He rises from attachment to things, to taking on the qualities of truth, and then to realizing the truth itself. — س قده

In the language of those who know God, a “point of arrival” is the station where the speaker is witnessed while someone recites His verses, as God reveals Himself through the quality expressed in each verse. Our master al-Ṣādiq said, “God has shown Himself to His servants in His speech, but they do not see Him.” One day, while praying, he fell unconscious. When asked why, he said, “I kept repeating a verse until I heard it from the One who spoke it.” Another version of the report says that every verse has an outer meaning and an inner meaning; every letter has a limit, and every limit has a point of arrival. The author may have quoted the meaning rather than the exact wording. — س قده

The “breast,” usually identified with the imagination, may have been added by a copyist. Without it, the list has seven levels. Another level, the deepest hidden one, may be added at the end; alternatively, one might leave out the intellect or nature. Nature would fit best here, since it is the outermost level. In short, these are terms used by those who follow the inward path. Philosophers often use “reasoning soul” for all or most of these levels. Those on the inward path often do not define them because, they say, they know them by direct experience. They explain them only as far as the subject allows. I gave their terms at the start of my notes on the first journey. — س قده
This means: know God through a light that comes from Him to your hearts. Draw near to Him until these words are true of you: “Through Me he sees, and through Me he hears.” — س قده

This means through the kind of prophecy that teaches people about God and His names. There are two kinds of prophecy: one that teaches God’s being, qualities, and names; and one that does all this while also bringing laws, teaching good character, and guiding public life. Some reserve the word “messengerhood” for the second kind. If so, the saying means inheriting the first kind of prophecy, as perfected people do. Even jurists can be its outward signs. A report says that whoever memorizes the Qur'an carries prophecy between his sides. Another report says that God has servants who are not prophets but whom the prophets envy. The Prophet also said that his community has people who receive insight and speak with angels. — س قده
This means becoming one of those entrusted with authority—not only people who know the truths, but also people able to act on them and bring about God’s commands in the world. — س قده

This means that the souls of beings such as luminous intellects and angels are not drawn to their own possibility, because the light of God’s eternal existence hides that possibility. The same is true of the intellects that rise toward God and lose sight of themselves in Him. Most people lean more toward possibility, and the effects of being many are stronger in them; outwardly or inwardly, they resemble those who deny the truth. Those who lean more toward existence, with a stronger sense of oneness, are among the prophets and saints who draw near to God. Those in whom the two sides are balanced are the moderate believers. — س قده
A beautiful line says: “Among those who love is a secret no word or pen can reveal.”

This refers to our prior being in the world of intellect. We are called “letters” because intellects do not exist independently; their existence depends entirely on God. They have no matter, or even a separate nature of their own, according to those who have understood this point. They belong to the divine realm, exist through God, and remain through Him. — س قده
This refers to our later being in the soul. — س قده

This means that the letters were like lines, extended in length and running straight down. Ibn Arabi says something similar: “We were lofty letters, not separate things, on the highest peaks.” The Commander of the Faithful said to Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī, “A word is a noun, a verb, and a letter,” pointing to the same truth. God’s “word” is His act, as the title of the chapter in Nahj al-Balāghah indicates. The word “Be!” refers to the existence that spreads through all things. It divides into the high letters of the intellect, the names—which are the lasting bodily beings—and the actions linked to time, which are changing qualities. In the author’s view, bodies also change in their very being. “Names” here means souls, which stand between still intellects and changing nature. — س قده

Different kinds of things, each with its own nature, are separated from one another and freed from foreign features. The individual things within each kind are then gathered into one whole. This is like the mind grasping the pure meaning of a thing, stripped of unrelated features. At that level, the meaning is one. The mind also separates qualities, amounts, positions, and other features that are mixed together in ordinary things. — س قده
This means the intellects, which are God’s speech and true word. — س قده

This means how the intellects become universal souls, which are God’s Book, and how they descend into open hearts. The universal soul is like a subtle copy of the intellect’s reality within the soul. It becomes simple images, without any loss or separation from its source. Another reading takes the three stages as knowledge held in one whole, knowledge unfolded in the soul, and images in the imagination. In short, “We made the word clear to them” refers to intellects becoming clear to other intellects; “a Book whose verses are clear” refers to the soul or imagination. — س قده
This includes the Qur'an as it exists in the intellect, in the soul, and in other forms, including God’s speech as it exists in His providential knowledge. — س قده

The point is that the world beyond the senses contains everything found here, including all five senses, in a form suited to that world. Each sense is reached by a matching inward sense. Through inward sight, the Prophet or saint sees what ordinary people cannot see; through inward hearing, he hears what they cannot hear. In the same way, he can taste, smell, and touch what ordinary people cannot. The Prophet said, “I spend the night with my Lord; He feeds and gives me drink.” He also said, “I can smell the breath of the Most Merciful from the direction of Yemen,” and, “I felt the coolness of his fingertips between my breasts.” These reports point to it. In short, when a prophet or saint leaves ordinary awareness, he perceives through inward senses, each suited to what it knows. — س قده

The pens here are not the intellects in the middle ranks, below the Highest Pen—whether that means the first intellect or the whole order of intellects. They are not the universal souls that govern the heavens either; those are the Preserved Tablet. The pens are the individual souls of the heavenly bodies. When viewed in relation to their bodies, they are tablets of erasure and confirmation, because their nature changes. When viewed as linked to their universal souls, they are pens that write on those tablets. — س قده

The Prophet’s connection with these souls is not always the same. At one time, he connects with the souls that know the positions and effects of the heavenly bodies, sees one set of forms, and draws one conclusion. At another time, he sees different forms and draws a different conclusion. — س قده

The author has said before that God’s activity has different levels. Ibn Arabi points to this by calling the changing movement of a heavenly soul “hesitation,” and linking it to a divine name such as “the Swift” or “the Shaper.” — س قده
That is, without the unseen, intellectual record of erasure and confirmation, there could be no actual erasure and confirmation in the changing world. — س قده

This explains “fixed within them.” The hesitation in people would be raised above them and become a fixed decree that could not be changed. Or it means that just as change comes from a divine reality, change in human souls is itself fixed by that reality. — س قده

As explained earlier, what makes us speak of something as not yet existing is its prior existence; what makes us speak of it as no longer existing is its later existence. Nonexistence is nothing in itself, so erasure does not mean that something is made into absolute nothing. Rather, one stage of a changing thing is erased and another is established, then that stage is erased and replaced. The Preserved Tablet and Highest Pen do not change. — س قده
Change takes place only on the two Tablets of Erasure and Confirmation: the unseen record and its visible counterpart. — س قده

The earlier “remarkable unveiling” is direct knowledge gained by thought and proof. The vision described here is an image seen through inner senses as a result of good actions and character. Every meaning has an image, and every reality has a subtle form. Those who follow the Prophet’s way can see these images through the inward senses. Some people, especially those who combine deep knowledge with spiritual practice, can bring together both kinds of vision. — س قده

This applies to the Qur'an as it exists in the world and within the human soul. In the revealed Qur'an, “wisdom” points to the fact that the whole Qur'an is contained in al-Fātiḥah, in the fourteen separate letters, in the bāʾ of “In the name of God,” and even in the dot beneath that letter. “Clear speech” points to its many levels: each chapter and verse has its own meaning. — س قده

This is clearer when applied to the Qur'an within the human soul than when applied to the written Qur'an, though the verse can include both. People were spiritually dead until God brought them to life by sending the Prophet, completing the work through the saint, and sending down the Qur'an. They were guided by its light. — س قده

This definition appears in The Healing and other works on divine philosophy. Wisdom is the best kind of knowledge because it gives certainty, not mere imitation. Other fields often rely on assumptions about their subjects, if not in every step then at least in accepting that their subjects exist. Divine philosophy has a leading place because its subject is existence itself, which is pure good; it studies God, His qualities and acts, the angels brought near to Him, and other beings that support the order of existence. Its goal is to make a person’s mind like the world and to reach true happiness. Its starting points are proofs that give lasting certainty. Its subject, goal, and starting points are all the best. The things it knows are therefore the best things to know. — س قده
This applies if wisdom means the highest form of direct knowledge, in which what is known is present to the knower. God alone has this knowledge in its fullest form, so wisdom is His gift. — س قده

The author relies here on the rule that higher causes are not completed by lower things, as his wording suggests. So “they had not already reached before acting” should mean prior in any sense, not only earlier in time. Separate higher causes do not gain perfection from actions that necessarily follow from their own nature. Their actions are blessings that flow from their being to what is below them. They have no goals in lower things for their own sake; if they did, those effects would complete them. Their goal is their own essence if nothing stands above them, as is true only of God, or a perfection above them, as is true of the separate intellects. Through their actions, the intellects imitate God by giving good, without needing the action or its results. This is pure generosity. That does not mean they are forced to act. They know their actions and approve of them because those actions fit their natures. An action of this kind is not coerced. Even if their actions follow necessarily from their natures, they still arise from knowledge and approval and are therefore chosen. — ط مد ظله

In short, providence brings together three things: knowledge, being a cause, and approval. We can clarify this by looking at what it means for us to take care over something. A person takes care to make an action happen, or to make it as complete as possible, without letting some other concern—more urgent, more loved, or more important—distract them from doing it. When we are busy with major matters, we may neglect small ones, either by not doing them at all or by not giving them all the care they need. If we give a small matter the same attention as a great one, or carefully manage all its needs and details as we would in a great matter, that is providence. We neglect small matters because we compare things. If two actions are required, one more important than the other, we may compare them, treat the more important one as the only real duty, and then neglect the less important one. Yet without that comparison, both would still be duties, and we would attend to the small one just as we attend to the large one. When we do not compare them, we know each action as it is: something required of us and suited to our nature. That is providence. It includes knowing the thing, causing it, and approving it because it fits the doer’s nature. God knows each thing as it is, without comparison or anything else weakening or changing that knowledge. He is the highest cause of every cause and its effects, and those effects fit His essence. So He has providence over all things. As this explanation shows, providence is normally an attribute of action: the fit between an action and its doer is understood from the action. But because that fit can be traced back to something in the essence, it can also be described as an attribute of essence. We can say that God’s essence knows things and causes them in a way that makes their effects fit Him. — ط مد ظله

We have already discussed eternal will. Tracing approval back to the special kind of causality by which effects fit their cause is more natural than explaining it as a separate will, which the author has already traced back to knowledge of the best order. — ط مد ظله

If the lack that belongs necessarily to every effect simply because it is possible were counted as “evil” in the technical sense, then the intellects—and even the heavenly spheres—could not be called wholly good when philosophers divide things into five groups to answer the dualists. On that usage, evil would be found only in the elemental world. The author will return to this technical meaning later. — س قده

This proof defies the critics, such as Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Rāzī and his followers, who said that philosophers had not proved that all existence is good and evil is a lack, but had relied only on isolated examples. The proof was given earlier by the scholar Shīrāzī in his commentary on The Wisdom of Illumination, before the author presented it here. It is a sound argument that is simple to follow, so the author accepted it. — س قده

Someone may ask: how can clouds blocking sunlight and rain preventing clothes from being bleached be examples of a harmful cause that does not reach the thing it harms? “Not reaching” means that the affected thing does not perceive the cause. And what is being harmed? The owner of the fruit or clothes; the harm is the loss of the benefit they need. The cause itself is perceived by touch or sight. — س قده

The power that perceives the harmful cause is not the power that suffers from it. The person’s sense of touch, which needs the sun’s warmth, cannot perceive the cloud. It perceives only the loss of health and warmth, and it judges that loss to be bad. Sight perceives the cloud, but the cloud does not harm sight. So the cloud is not itself judged evil by the power that perceives it; what is judged evil is the loss of health and warmth. The sense that can see the cloud is not harmed by it, while the sense that is harmed does not perceive it. If the cloud were evil in itself, it would make the perceiving sense suffer. This shows again that evil belongs to a lack. — س قده
This takes an unnecessary detour. Pain’s existence is known directly from experience; there is no need to prove that it exists by first saying that it is a kind of perception. — س قده

The reply does not seem to resolve the problem. First, the objection is broader than direct sense perception. The severed limb is only an example. The claim that pain is direct awareness of a lack does not explain pain caused by knowing that loved ones have died, or by other thoughts and judgements. Second, it is hard to say that sense perception is always direct awareness of the thing itself when the senses often make mistakes about the outside world. Saying that all knowledge is direct in some deeper way does not help, because that concerns knowledge as it is in itself, not whether it matches what exists outside us. The problem can instead be answered this way: the mental image that causes pain is not evil insofar as it perfects the person’s knowledge. In that respect it is something good that exists. But insofar as it represents what has happened outside us—such as a limb being severed or a connection being broken—it is tied to a lack. The evil is in that lack, not in the mental image. — ط مد ظله

The scholar Dawānī did not say that the only thing perceived is a broken connection, so it is not enough to answer that pain is a kind of direct perception and that perception is identical with what it perceives. He can say: even if direct awareness is identical with its object, we have not agreed that the only object perceived is the broken connection. That absence is perceived, as other absences are, but what we call pain is the single, present state of hurt that is felt. It is not the broken connection itself—especially when pain comes from an unhealthy bodily condition. How can that felt state be a lack? A lack, simply as a lack, has no awareness or effect, yet this painful state has both. The author himself says in his discussion of motion and rest that each thing has its own kind of existence, and that motion and relations exist in the world. If motion, relation, and other weak kinds of existence are still existents, why should pain not be an existent too? Some philosophers say pain is caused by a broken connection; others say it is caused by an unhealthy bodily state. Feeling the broken connection is awareness of the cause of pain, while feeling the hurt itself is awareness of the painful state. Since pain exists, they also question how an absence, such as a broken connection, can cause something that exists. They have tried to avoid this problem by treating the broken connection as something that exists. The true answer to Dawānī’s objection is this. What pain makes us directly aware of may be either a lack, such as a broken connection, in which case evil is a lack, as the author says; or a positive state, as the objector proposes and as we also allowed as a possibility. In that case, pain as an existing hurt is good in itself. A thing can be good in itself without being pleasant to a particular person. The fact that someone’s weakness makes a state unpleasant to them does not make it evil in itself. How could that existence be evil in its own nature when every kind of existence fits its own nature? A body calls for existence with potential multiplicity; a separate number calls for many actual units; a continuous whole calls for a connected existence; something that changes calls for an existence that changes; fire calls for an active, penetrating existence; snake venom calls for a biting, painful existence. None of these is evil in itself or by its nature. The same is true of pain. We cannot call these things evil in their own nature because a thing is evil only when it harms the existence or perfection of something already present. But here we are speaking of what each kind of thing calls for in itself from the beginning, in the fixed realities of things, which are known through God’s pure giving. There, pain is not evil in itself. It is evil only in relation to those who receive it and are affected by it. This is shown by the fact that, in God’s knowledge, which is direct and identical with what is known, pain is not called evil: God’s knowledge is active and wholly good, and He is not affected or changed. We can see that pain is called evil in our knowledge not because it is an act of awareness or an existing thing, but because it affects us and changes us. Pain also brings many further goods. It can help the blessed and those brought near to God reach high states of patience, approval, and surrender. Seeing pain also lets us understand the condition of those who suffer, so that we can help them and be helped. These benefits, as well as its existence, show that the argument needs to be answered by the distinction given here. — س قده

The author uses three claims to show that pain is a lack like a broken connection: first, that awareness of what opposes us is direct, not through a mental image; second, that a thing’s existence is identical with what it is; and third, that knowledge of a thing is identical with the thing known in itself. Even if all three claims are true, they answer only one of the two perceptions: awareness of the broken connection, not the pain caused by it. The objection assumes that the two can occur separately. The real answer is the one given here: pain and hurt are positive things that exist, and are good in themselves, even when they are unpleasant to the person who feels them. — س قده

If what is missing is the thing itself, then the thing’s essence is what is described as absent. If what is missing is one of its perfections, then it is the essence of that existing thing that is described as lacking that perfection. — ط مد

Someone might say that a human being feels more pain than an animal when struck with a stick. The answer is that the author means the soul, as a soul, is less harmed, while the living animal body, as a body, is harmed more. He added that condition to distinguish the soul from an animal’s soul, which has some freedom from matter through imagination. And if human beings seem to suffer more, it may be because their bodies are more delicate and their senses sharper than those of animals. — س قده

This division is attributed to Aristotle. It does not conflict with the claim that evil is a lack, since, as explained earlier, evil is a lack that belongs to a particular thing and therefore has some connection with existence. — ط مد

The author gives the division before returning to the proof. The proof later shows that some of these groups do not exist and so are not among the kinds that actually occur. Here, good and evil may mean either what is good or evil in itself, or what is good or evil in relation to something else. A passage in The Glimmers suggests the second meaning. It first says that the first group contains no evil “in relation to anything,” and then gives as examples the intellects, which have no potentiality and do not harm any other being. — س قده

The author may have realized that tracing evil to absence would mean that it occurs in every possible essence, since an essence can be the source of absences and losses. It would also mean that evil occurs at every level of existence: each lower level lacks some perfection of the level above it. So it seems that evil must be more common than good in the order of creation. He replies that the “evil” discussed here, in the agreed technical sense, means the absence of a thing or one of its perfections. A thing must have the potential to be absent, or to lose its perfection, and that is matter. Evil is therefore found only in the material world. But defining the word this way does not solve the real problem. The analysis still seems to show that absence and evil exist at levels beyond matter. The author has repeatedly said that possibility, essence, every lack, and every limit are privative in nature, and that absence is evil. The sounder answer is to admit that possible existence always includes a kind of evil, though some evil is only relative: for example, a possible thing is lacking when compared with the Necessary Existent, and each level of existence is lacking when compared with the level above it. This kind of lack is part of what the thing is and does not come from divine decree. A different kind of lack, such as death or losing a perfection after having it, is limited to matter. The author answers that kind in the main text. — ط مد ظله

This explains why evil occurs according to the philosophers’ view of generation and decay, where one form replaces another. In the author’s view of substantial motion, one basic form does not lose any perfection when another form follows it, whether the later form is higher, such as an animal form following a human form, or another form at the same level. Evil is the loss of a stage or limit in the moving matter, when compared with that matter’s continuing potential. This loss is a necessary part of change; it is not separately caused. Qualities that depend on basic forms change along with them, so the same reasoning applies to the loss of these qualities. — ط مد
